analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers sell individual health plans across state lines under the rules of whichever state they choose.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee in July 2009 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let a health insurance company pick one state as its "primary state" and sell individual health insurance in every other state under that state's rules, rather than the rules of the state where the buyer lives. The buyer's own state could not apply its insurance laws to the plan, except for a short list of protections like financial solvency checks and fraud enforcement. Insurers would have to disclose in bold print that the cheaper policy may not cover services or include consumer protections the buyer's state requires, and a few federal floor rules would apply, such as bans on health-status premium increases at renewal and access to independent review of denied claims. The bill was introduced by Rep. John Shadegg with 28 Republican cosponsors and never received a committee vote or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurers selling individual health policies gain the most: they could pick the state with the loosest rules and sell that same product nationwide, escaping state-mandated benefits, rate restrictions, and medical underwriting limits. Consumers who are healthy and buy their own insurance could gain access to cheaper, bare-bones plans. People with pre-existing conditions would likely pay more in their own states' markets as healthier buyers migrate to the cheap out-of-state plans.

how_it_helps.text: It would let an insurer sell an individual health plan in every state under the rules of a single state it designates as its 'primary state,' instead of complying with 50 different sets of state insurance laws.

The bill's stated finding is that variation among state laws raises the cost of individual coverage, and that letting insurers sell nationwide under one state's rules would increase efficiency and lower prices.

It includes some consumer guardrails: a bold-print notice telling buyers the policy may lack their state's mandated benefits and consumer protections, a ban on raising a person's premium at renewal based on their health status, guaranteed availability for HIPAA-eligible individuals where a state lacks a high-risk pool, and required independent external review of denied claims.

analysis.who_pays: People who buy the cheaper out-of-state plans bear the risk of thinner coverage — fewer mandated benefits, weaker consumer protections, and no limits from their own state on rate changes. Residents who stay in their state's market could face rising premiums as healthier people leave that pool. State governments lose regulatory authority over plans sold to their own residents.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick residents and buyers of thin plans

drawbacks.text: Policies sold into a state would only have to meet the rules of the insurer's chosen 'primary state,' so plans could legally omit benefits a buyer's own state requires and could not be blocked by that state's insurance regulators.

The bill text's own mandatory disclosure warns buyers that such a policy 'may be less expensive than others because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws' of their state, 'including coverage of some services or benefits mandated' by that state, and is 'not subject to all of the consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes.'

States could not restrict medical underwriting in these out-of-state plans, so sick residents could be priced out of the cheaper interstate market, and critics have long argued this dynamic would deepen the divide between cheap plans for the healthy and unaffordable coverage for everyone else.

Because a federal law preempts state rules, a state with strong consumer protections could not stop weaker out-of-state plans from being sold to its residents, and enforcement of most rules would sit with the distant primary state rather than the buyer's home state.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would make cheaper, skimpier policies available, which helps healthy people who currently find insurance unaffordable and might accept thinner coverage. The cost falls on people who buy those policies without realizing what is missing, and especially on anyone who becomes sick, since the lower-priced market relies on healthier buyers; if premiums for the sick rise further, the bill shifts risk from insurers and healthy enrollees onto the least healthy. The disclosure notice mitigates but does not remove the risk of consumers buying coverage that fails them when they need it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittees in July 2009, no committee or floor vote ever happened, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 14, 2009 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to two subcommittees — Health, and Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection — and no further action was ever taken.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote occurred before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill never advanced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State insurance regulators and insurers built around state-by-state rules, since the state regulatory system stayed intact; consumers shopping for cheaper coverage did not get the option.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State regulators and the status quo insurance system

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair Henry Waxman, D-CA)
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill sat in a Democratic-controlled committee without a vote.

industries.note: Insurers gain the right to sell individual policies nationwide under the single state's rules they choose, avoiding the regulatory requirements of every other state — including mandated benefits, rate restrictions, and underwriting limits. The notice, external-review, and financial requirements add compliance costs but do not change the core benefit.

States lose their power to regulate the terms of individual health plans sold to their own residents when the insurer designates another state as primary; their role shrinks to financial examinations, fraud and claims-practice enforcement, and tax collection.

industries.industry: State-regulated insurers competing only in their home market
industries.note: Regional insurers that currently benefit from state-by-state markets would face competition from national sellers operating under the most permissive state's rules.
